purpose: Educational OSINT tool for learning deep/dark web concepts without accessing illicit content
legal_disclaimer: This tool uses only synthetic data and publicly documented concepts for educational purposes. It does not access the dark web or any illicit content.

modules.title: Surface vs Deep vs Dark Web

definitions.surface_web: Public websites indexed by search engines (Google, Bing). Examples: news sites, social media, e-commerce.
definitions.deep_web: Content not indexed by search engines. Includes email inboxes, paywalled content, private databases, internal portals. ~90%+ of internet.
definitions.dark_web: Hidden subset of deep web requiring special software (Tor). Uses .onion domains. Designed for anonymity. Hosts both legitimate privacy services and illicit markets.

key_differences: Surface web: indexed, public, standard browsers
Deep web: unindexed, private/auth-required, standard browsers
Dark web: hidden, anonymized, requires Tor/special protocols

quiz.question: Which layer of the web includes your email inbox?
quiz.explanation: Email inboxes are not indexed by search engines and require authentication, making them part of the deep web.

quiz.question: What software is required to access .onion domains?
quiz.explanation: .onion domains are only accessible through the Tor Browser or compatible Tor clients.

quiz.question: True or False: The dark web and deep web are the same thing.
quiz.explanation: They are different. The deep web is all unindexed content; the dark web is a small, anonymized subset requiring special software.

illicit_markets.description: Marketplaces selling stolen credentials, malware, phishing kits, exploits
illicit_markets.detection_relevance: Source of initial access tools, credential stuffing campaigns, phishing infrastructure

forums.description: Discussion boards for threat actors to share TTPs, tools, and coordinate
forums.detection_relevance: Early indicators of campaigns, tool development, vendor targeting

privacy_services.description: Legitimate anonymity tools, secure email, censorship-resistant hosting
privacy_services.detection_relevance: Understanding dual-use infrastructure; not all dark web activity is malicious

whistleblowing.description: Secure drop sites for journalists and activists
whistleblowing.detection_relevance: Legitimate use cases; important for threat intel context

mirrors.description: Censorship-resistant mirrors of surface-web services (news, social media)
mirrors.detection_relevance: Understanding onion service architecture; some are legitimate

quiz.question: Which dark-web service type is most relevant for early campaign indicators?
quiz.explanation: Forums often contain discussions about upcoming campaigns, tool development, and targeting strategies.

quiz.question: True or False: All dark-web services are illegal.
quiz.explanation: False. Many dark-web services are legitimate privacy tools, news mirrors, or whistleblowing platforms.

ttps.name: Credential Stuffing from Leaked Databases
ttps.description: Threat actors purchase leaked credentials from dark-web markets and automate login attempts across multiple services.
ttps.detection_hypothesis: High volume of failed logins from diverse IPs targeting same accounts; geographic anomalies in login attempts

synthetic_indicators.pattern: Multiple failed logins (>10) within 5 minutes from geographically dispersed IPs

ttps.name: Phishing Kit Distribution via Dark-Web Markets
ttps.description: Ready-to-deploy phishing kits (landing pages, credential harvesters, email templates) sold on dark-web marketplaces.
ttps.detection_hypothesis: Newly registered domains with lookalike branding; suspicious email attachments with credential harvesting forms

synthetic_indicators.pattern: Domains registered <7 days ago with typosquatting patterns targeting financial brands

ttps.name: Initial Access Brokering
ttps.description: Threat actors sell access to compromised corporate networks (via RDP, VPN, web shells) acquired through dark-web channels.
ttps.detection_hypothesis: Unusual RDP/VPN connections from unexpected geolocations; web shell artifacts on internet-facing servers

synthetic_indicators.log_example: 2026-10-02 03:22:05 VPN_CONNECT user=svc_backup src_ip=45.155.205.89 geo=NL time=03:22 local_time=22:22_prev_day
synthetic_indicators.pattern: Service account VPN connections from non-corporate IPs during off-hours

ttps.name: Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS)
ttps.description: Ransomware, info-stealers, and RATs offered via subscription or affiliate programs on dark-web forums.
ttps.detection_hypothesis: Known malware signatures; suspicious PowerShell/LOLBin usage; C2 beaconing patterns

synthetic_indicators.pattern: Encoded PowerShell commands spawned from office applications or browsers

detection_exercise.scenario: You observe the following log entries in your SIEM over a 2-hour window. Identify which TTP(s) might be occurring and write a detection rule.

detection_rule_template.name: Credential Stuffing Followed by Suspicious PowerShell
detection_rule_template.logic: ALERT IF (failed_logins > 10 within 5 minutes for same user) AND (success_login from same IP as failed attempts) AND (powershell.exe spawned from office app with encoded command)
detection_rule_template.false_positives: Legitimate penetration testing; password manager testing; user traveling internationally

scenario.title: Investigate a Dark-Web Mention in Threat Intel Report
scenario.background: Your threat intel team received a report mentioning a new phishing kit being sold on a dark-web marketplace. The report includes a synthetic .onion address and vendor name.

workflow_steps.guidance: Check if the threat intel vendor is reputable. Look for corroborating reports from other vendors.
Search for the vendor name and .onion address in public sources (news, blogs, forums).

mentions_found.context: Mentioned as new phishing kit vendor
Analyzed sample attributed to DarkPhish Pro

workflow_steps.guidance: Search for phishing campaigns using similar TTPs or infrastructure in your telemetry.
Based on claimed capabilities, what would you expect to see in logs?

hypotheses: Increased phishing emails with banking-themed lures
PowerShell downloads from newly registered domains
C2 beaconing to IPs in bulletproof hosting ranges

workflow_steps.guidance: Create a brief intelligence summary for your team.

synthetic_output.summary_template: A new phishing kit vendor 'DarkPhish Pro' has been reported selling banking trojans on dark-web marketplaces since 2026-09-15. Corroborating reports from 3 sources suggest active campaigns. Recommend monitoring for [hypotheses list] and updating email filtering rules for banking-themed lures.

final_quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a legitimate use case for the dark web?
final_quiz.explanation: Selling stolen credentials is illegal. Whistleblowing, news mirrors, and secure email are legitimate privacy-focused uses.

final_quiz.question: What is the primary detection hypothesis for credential stuffing attacks?
options: Single failed login from unusual location
Multiple failed logins from diverse IPs targeting same accounts
final_quiz.explanation: Credential stuffing involves automated login attempts from many IPs against the same accounts, resulting in high volumes of failed logins.

final_quiz.question: In the OSINT workflow, what is the first step after receiving dark-web threat intel?
options: Validate the source and check for corroboration
final_quiz.explanation: Always validate the source and look for corroborating reports before taking action or investing investigation time.

example_solution.logic: ALERT IF (email contains banking-themed subject line) AND (attachment is HTML/JS with external form POST) AND (sender domain registered <7 days ago)
false_positives: Legitimate marketing campaigns from new domains
Password reset emails from newly configured services
